entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a sine wave by converting it into positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials and identifying the nonzero harmonic coefficients that determine its magnitude and phase spectra.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave

blocks.text: Start from the complex Fourier series form $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$. For the unit-amplitude, zero-phase sine wave $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ with period $T_0=2\pi/\omega_0$, the target is to show that only two harmonic slots matter.

Use Euler's identity for sine to rewrite the signal in terms of the positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials. That rewrite is the key recognition step, because it shows the sine wave already has the exact basis functions used in the Fourier series.

The term $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ matches the $k=1$ basis function, and the term $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ matches the $k=-1$ basis function. So the sine wave places all of its Fourier-series weight on those two harmonics and nowhere else.

Read that coefficient pattern as the whole story for the base case: a unit sine wave produces one positive-harmonic coefficient and one negative-harmonic coefficient with equal magnitude and opposite sign. Later sections will keep the same two-harmonic structure and only rescale or rotate those coefficients when amplitude or phase changes.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine Wave into Complex Exponentials

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ as a sum of positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the unit-amplitude, zero-phase sine wave $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ as the base case. The cue is the fundamental-frequency sine, and the job is to rewrite it in the same exponential basis used by the complex Fourier series.

Here $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ is the $k=1$ harmonic basis function and $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ is the $k=-1$ harmonic basis function. No other harmonics appear in this rewrite, so the sine wave is already isolated to its two fundamental-frequency slots.

This is the exponential form we want: the sine wave is now written as one positive-frequency term and one negative-frequency term, with no extra harmonic content. The next step will read those two terms as the only nonzero Fourier coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Identifying the k = 1 and k = -1 Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=\frac{1}{2j}e^{j\omega_0 t}-\frac{1}{2j}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, identify the nonzero Fourier coefficients.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the rewritten exponential form. The positive-frequency term $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ belongs to the $k=1$ slot, and the negative-frequency term $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ belongs to the $k=-1$ slot, so each coefficient is read directly from the factor in front of its harmonic basis function.

If useful, simplify those coefficients into rectangular form: $\frac{1}{2j}=-\frac{j}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2j}=\frac{j}{2}$. No other harmonics appear in the exponential form, so every coefficient except the $k=\pm1$ pair is zero.

This coefficient pair is the complete Fourier-series signature of the unit sine wave: one nonzero positive-harmonic coefficient and one nonzero negative-harmonic coefficient with matching magnitude and opposite sign pattern. The next steps will change amplitude or phase, but they will keep the same two harmonic slots.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Including Amplitude in Sine-Wave Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Find the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the amplitude-scaled sine wave $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t)$. The cue is the same fundamental-frequency sine as before, but now the entire waveform is multiplied by $A$, so the coefficient pair should be scaled by that same factor.
Because amplitude multiplies the whole signal, it multiplies both harmonic slots equally. So the $k=1$ term becomes $c_1=\frac{A}{2j}$ and the $k=-1$ term becomes $c_{-1}=-\frac{A}{2j}$.

That is the whole effect of amplitude in this case: the two nonzero coefficients are the unit-sine coefficients scaled by $A$, and no new harmonics appear. The next variation will keep the same two slots and change how the coefficients rotate with phase.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Including Sinusoidal Phase in the Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Find the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the phase-shifted sine wave $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$. The cue is the same two-slot harmonic pattern as before; the only new ingredient is that the phase sits inside each exponential and rotates the coefficients.
Separate the phase from the time factor so the Fourier-series slots are visible. This gives one $k=1$ term and one $k=-1$ term, each multiplied by its own complex phase factor.

The phase changes the complex values of the two nonzero coefficients, not their locations. The harmonic pattern is still limited to $k=\pm 1$, so the only effect of $\phi$ is to rotate the coefficient pair in opposite directions.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Reading Magnitude and Phase from Sine-Wave Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: From the coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$, determine the magnitude and phase spectrum entries at $k=\pm1$ and state which harmonics are nonzero.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the nonzero coefficient pair for the phase-shifted sine wave. The cue is a two-line spectrum, so read magnitude from absolute value and phase from the coefficient angle.
Take magnitudes first. Both nonzero harmonics have the same magnitude because the phase factors have unit length, so the magnitude spectrum has equal lines at $k=1$ and $k=-1$.

Now read the phases. The $k=1$ line has angle $\phi-\frac{\pi}{2}$, while the $k=-1$ line has angle $\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi$ modulo $2\pi$. The phase shift rotates the two lines in opposite directions, but it does not create any new harmonics.
So the spectrum is sparse: two equal magnitude lines at $k=\pm1$, with opposite phase rotations set by $\phi$, and every other coefficient is zero.

entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a rectangular periodic signal by recognizing that only the pulse-support interval contributes to the one-period coefficient integral and evaluating the resulting exponential integral in terms of amplitude, width, period, and harmonic index.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal

blocks.text: For a rectangular periodic signal with amplitude $A$, pulse width $\tau$, and period $T$, the complex Fourier coefficient formula uses the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=2\pi/T$. The base case is a single pulse per period: the signal equals $A$ on the pulse-support interval and is $0$ everywhere else in the period.

Because the signal is zero outside the pulse, only the pulse-support interval can contribute to the integral. That means we can replace the full-period description with the piecewise rectangular form and focus only on the interval $0\le t<\tau$.

With that description in place, the one-period coefficient integral collapses to the pulse-support interval, and the constant amplitude factors out immediately. This is the step that turns a full-period integral into a short, reusable expression in $A$, $\tau$, $T$, and $k$.

From here, the nonzero-harmonic case comes from evaluating the exponential antiderivative on the support interval. The special case $k=0$ is the average value over one period, so it stays separate from the $k\ne0$ formula.

The reusable pattern is simple: identify the pulse support, restrict the coefficient integral to that interval, factor out the constant amplitude, and then use the same exponential integral for every nonzero harmonic. Once the support interval is recognized, the coefficient formula becomes a short expression in $A$, $\tau$, $T$, and $k$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Reading Amplitude, Pulse Width, and Period from a Rectangular Signal

image_slots.image_description: A clean rectangular periodic signal plot with one pulse per period. Show a single pulse starting at t=0, with height labeled 3, horizontal width labeled 2, and the next identical pulse beginning 8 time units later so the period is clearly 8. Label the time axis. Highlight the pulse-support interval 0 <= t < 2. Keep the plot uncluttered, educational, and visually centered on the parameter-reading task.

example_content.example_prompt: A rectangular periodic signal is shown with height $3$, pulse width $2$, and period $8$. Read off $A$, $\tau$, and $T$ from the plot.

explanation_blocks.text: When a signal is a repeated rectangular pulse, read the amplitude from the pulse height, the pulse width from the on-interval, and the period from the spacing between identical pulses. This plot gives one clean pulse per period, so the three numbers can be read directly from the picture before any coefficient computation starts.
The pulse reaches a height of $3$, so the amplitude is $A=3$. The pulse runs from $t=0$ to $t=2$, so the pulse width is $\tau=2$.
The next identical pulse begins $8$ time units later, so the period is $T=8$. The rectangular signal is now fully specified by the parameter triple $(A,\tau,T)=(3,2,8)$.

This is the only information needed from the plot at this step: identify the height, the on-interval, and the repeat spacing. Once those three values are read correctly, the rectangular signal is fully specified for this example.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Restricting the Coefficient Integral to the Pulse Support

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ on $\tau\le t<T$, rewrite the coefficient integral so it runs only over the pulse support.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the one-period Fourier coefficient formula. The only new cue in this step is the pulse support: $x(t)$ is constant on $0\le t<\tau$ and zero everywhere else in the period.
Substitute the piecewise definition of the rectangular signal and split the integral at the pulse boundary. The second interval carries no contribution because $x(t)=0$ there.

explanation_blocks.latex: c_k = \frac{1}{T}\left(\int_0^\tau A e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt + \int_\tau^T 0\cdot e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt\right)

explanation_blocks.text: Drop the zero-valued interval and factor out the constant amplitude $A$. The full-period coefficient integral collapses to the pulse-support integral.
This restricted form is the pattern to reuse: keep the coefficient kernel, keep the support interval, and ignore the rest of the period because it contributes nothing.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Exponential Integral for Nonzero Harmonics

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$, compute $c_1$ by evaluating the restricted exponential integral.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the restricted-support form from the previous step, then set $k=1$ for the first nonzero harmonic. The only task now is to evaluate the exponential integral on $0\le t<\tau$.

Antidifferentiate $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ as $\frac{e^{-j\omega_0 t}}{-j\omega_0}$ and evaluate it at the pulse endpoints. This keeps the amplitude factor outside the integral and uses the support interval as the only integration range.
Rewrite the difference in the standard nonzero-harmonic form. The result is a closed-form coefficient in terms of $A$, $\tau$, $T$, and $\omega_0$.
This is the pattern to reuse for any nonzero harmonic: substitute the index, integrate the exponential on the support interval, and simplify the endpoint difference.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Writing Rectangular-Signal Coefficients Using Amplitude, Width, Period, and Harmonic Index

example_content.example_prompt: For a rectangular periodic signal that equals $A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$, write the formula for $c_k$ and separate the $k=0$ case from the $k\ne0$ case.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the restricted-support result and keep the harmonic index symbolic for now. The coefficient has one special case at $k=0$ and one closed form for $k\ne0$.
For the DC term, set $k=0$ before evaluating the integral. That turns the coefficient into the pulse area divided by the period.
Now replace $\omega_0$ with $2\pi/T$ and combine the two cases into one formula. The result is expressed entirely with $A$, $\tau$, $T$, and $k$.
That is the reusable rectangular-signal coefficient formula: one average-value coefficient at $k=0$ and one exponential closed form for every $k\ne0$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC Fourier-series coefficient for a rectangular periodic signal by converting duty cycle and signal levels into the average value over one period.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Duty Cycle and DC Value

blocks.text: For a rectangular periodic signal, the duty cycle $D$ is the fraction of each period that the signal spends at the high level. If the signal is high for a time $\tau$ inside a period $T$, then $D = \frac{\tau}{T}$.
The DC Fourier-series coefficient is the average value over one period. For a periodic signal $x(t)$, compute that average by integrating over one full period and dividing by $T$.

In the simplest pulse train, $x(t)=A$ on the on-time of length $\tau$ and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere. Only the high interval contributes to the integral, so the average becomes the high level times the duty cycle.

So the rule to carry forward is simple: read the duty cycle from the on-time, then take the one-period average to get the DC value. Later rectangular signals will use the same average-value idea, even when the signal levels change.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value from a Given Duty Cycle

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $12$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of each period and $0$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the duty cycle is already given: $D=\frac{1}{3}$. The signal is high for that fraction of each period and $0$ for the rest, so the DC value is the one-period average.
The high level contributes $12$ for the first third of the period, and the low level contributes $0$ for the remaining two thirds. So the average becomes the high level times the duty cycle.
So the DC value is $4$. In Fourier-series language, that average is the DC coefficient for this rectangular signal.

sections.section_title: Finding Duty Cycle from Pulse Width and Period

example_content.example_prompt: A rectangular signal is high for $2$ ms of every $5$ ms period and is $0$ otherwise. If the high level is $10$, what is its DC value?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the pulse width and period are already given: the signal is high for $2$ ms out of every $5$ ms period. That means the first step is to convert the geometry into duty cycle $D = \tau/T$.

Now use the average-value formula for the rectangular signal. With high level $10$ and low level $0$, the DC value is the high level weighted by the high-time fraction and the low level weighted by the remaining fraction.
Simplifying gives $\bar{x}=4$. So the DC value is $4$, and the key move is converting pulse width and period into duty cycle before averaging.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value for a Two-Level Rectangular Signal

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $6$ for $\frac{1}{4}$ of each period and $-1$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a two-level rectangular signal. The high level is $6$ for a fraction $\frac{1}{4}$ of the period, so the low level $-1$ fills the remaining $\frac{3}{4}$.
Now simplify each contribution. The high level contributes $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$, and the low level contributes $-\frac{3}{4}$.
So the DC value is $\frac{3}{4}$. The key move is the weighted average of the two levels, with each level multiplied by the fraction of time it appears.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero DC Value from Balanced Signal Levels

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $4$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of each period and $-2$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal has two levels and the weighted contributions are meant to cancel. The high level is $4$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of the period, so the low level $-2$ fills the remaining $\frac{2}{3}$.
Now compare the two weighted terms. The positive contribution is $\frac{4}{3}$, and the negative contribution is $-\frac{4}{3}$, so they have equal magnitude and opposite sign.
So the DC value is $0$. The key recognition is that balanced weighted levels cancel exactly, so the average over one period is zero.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify coefficient cancellations in the Fourier series coefficient formula to determine which even and odd harmonic indices of a periodic signal contribute nonzero spectral components.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Even and Odd Harmonics

blocks.text: When a Fourier-series coefficient formula contains $(-1)^k$, test the parity of $k$ before you simplify anything else. Write even harmonics as $k = 2m$ and odd harmonics as $k = 2m + 1$, and keep $k = 0$ separate as the DC term.
That parity split is what makes cancellation visible in coefficient formulas. A factor like $1 + (-1)^k$ survives on even indices and vanishes on odd indices, while $1 - (-1)^k$ does the opposite.

So the operational test is simple: inspect the coefficient formula, substitute the even form $k = 2m$ and the odd form $k = 2m + 1$, simplify the parity factor, and list the harmonic indices whose coefficients stay nonzero.

sections.section_title: Identifying Even and Odd Harmonic Indices

example_content.example_prompt: Given the indices $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, identify the even harmonic indices, the odd harmonic indices, and the DC term.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the index list $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$. The task here is classification: decide which indices are even, which are odd, and keep $k = 0$ separate as the DC term.

explanation_blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}k = 0 &\text{ is the DC term} \\ k = 2, 4, 6 &\text{ are the even harmonic indices} \\ k = 1, 3, 5 &\text{ are the odd harmonic indices}\end{aligned}

explanation_blocks.text: So the even harmonic set is $\{2, 4, 6\}$ and the odd harmonic set is $\{1, 3, 5\}$. That bookkeeping is the piece you will reuse later when a coefficient formula tells you which parity survives and which parity cancels.

sections.section_title: Detecting Even-Harmonic Cancellations

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_k = A(1 - (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, determine which harmonic indices are zero and which survive.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor $1 - (-1)^k$ inside the coefficient formula. Test it on even and odd positive indices, then read off which parity class makes the factor vanish.
So $c_{2m} = 0$ for every even harmonic index, while $c_{2m+1} = 2A$ for every odd harmonic index. The surviving set is the odd harmonics.

sections.section_title: Detecting Odd-Harmonic Cancellations

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_k = A(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, determine which harmonic indices are zero and which survive.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor $1 + (-1)^k$ inside the coefficient formula. Test it on even and odd positive indices, then read off which parity class makes the factor vanish. The only change from the previous case is the sign, and that swaps the surviving family.
So $c_{2m+1} = 0$ for every odd harmonic index, while $c_{2m} = 2A$ for every even harmonic index. The surviving set is the even harmonics.

sections.section_title: Listing Nonzero Harmonics from a Coefficient Formula

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_k = A(1 - (-1)^k) + B(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, determine which harmonic families are nonzero and list the surviving even and odd harmonics.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the full coefficient formula with one factor that cancels even harmonics and one factor that cancels odd harmonics. Test the even and odd positive indices separately, then name every parity class that survives.

So neither parity class cancels completely. The even harmonics survive through the $B$ term, and the odd harmonics survive through the $A$ term, so the nonzero harmonic families are both even and odd.

entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier-series coefficient integral for one period of an exponentially shaped periodic signal by combining the signal exponent with the harmonic kernel to obtain each harmonic coefficient.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential

blocks.text: A periodic complex exponential such as $x(t)=e^{jm\omega_0 t}$ on $0 \le t < T$ is already a single Fourier harmonic. In this section, the goal is to see which coefficient survives when we apply the coefficient formula over one period.

Use the standard period relation $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ so the coefficient is measured over exactly one cycle. That keeps the setup tied to one full period and makes the matching-harmonic test meaningful.
Now substitute $x(t)=e^{jm\omega_0 t}$ into the integral. The two exponentials combine, and the exponent becomes the difference $m-k$.

That difference tells you the two outcomes to watch for later: if $m-k=0$, the matching harmonic remains; if $m-k\ne0$, the exponential averages away over the full period. The next step will use that split to evaluate specific coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Setting Up the One-Period Coefficient Integral

example_content.example_prompt: For the periodic exponential $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ over one period $0 \le t < T$, set up the complex Fourier-series coefficient integral for $c_2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a periodic complex exponential on one full period, so the right starting point is the standard one-period Fourier coefficient formula. Keep the normalization factor and the full-period limits exactly as written, with $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}$.
Now specialize to the given signal $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ and the target coefficient $c_2$. Substitute the signal and the harmonic kernel $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, but do not simplify the exponent yet.

This is the complete setup: the coefficient is written over one full period, the $1/T$ factor is present, and the harmonic kernel is left intact for the next step. The only job here is to set up the integral correctly.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Combining Exponents in the Integrand

example_content.example_prompt: For the same periodic exponential $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, combine the signal exponential and the harmonic kernel in the coefficient integral for $c_2$ and rewrite the integrand as one exponential.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the setup in Section 2. The cue is the product inside $c_2$: the periodic exponential $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ times the harmonic kernel $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$.
Multiply the exponentials by adding exponents. Here the signal index is $m=3$ and the harmonic index is $k=2$, so the exponent becomes $j(m-k)\omega_0 t=j(3-2)\omega_0 t$.
The integrand is now a single complex exponential with the mismatch made explicit. That is the form the next step can integrate directly.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Evaluating Coefficients When the Combined Exponent Is Nonzero

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, evaluate $c_2$ by integrating the nonzero combined exponent over one period and showing that the result cancels to zero.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the simplified integrand in Section 3. The cue is the single exponential $e^{j(3-2)\omega_0 t}=e^{j\omega_0 t}$ inside the one-period coefficient integral.
Integrate the exponential directly. An antiderivative is $\frac{1}{j\omega_0}e^{j\omega_0 t}$, so the coefficient is the endpoint difference divided by $T$.
Now use $\omega_0T=2\pi$. The upper limit gives $e^{j\omega_0T}=e^{j2\pi}=1$, so the endpoint terms cancel and the nonmatching coefficient is zero.
The result is the expected full-period cancellation: a nonzero combined exponent still averages to zero over one period when the harmonic does not match the signal index.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Coefficient When the Combined Exponent Is Zero

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, evaluate $c_3$ when the combined exponent is zero.

explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=3$ so the combined exponent is $j(3-3)\omega_0 t=0$. The cue is the constant integrand $1$ inside the one-period coefficient integral.
Because the integrand is constant, the integral over one period is $T$, and the outer factor $1/T$ cancels it.
The matching harmonic survives with coefficient $1$. That is the zero-exponent case that contrasts with the previous nonmatching branch.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute complex-valued Fourier series coefficients by evaluating the one-period complex-exponential coefficient integral and interpreting each result as the harmonic's amplitude-and-phase weight.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex-Valued Fourier Coefficients

blocks.text: A complex Fourier series writes a periodic signal as $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$. The index $k$ labels the harmonic, and $\omega_0$ is the fundamental angular frequency.

To find one coefficient, multiply by the matching exponential $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$ and average over one period $T$. That one-period projection isolates the $k$th harmonic and gives its complex weight $c_k$.

Start with a constant signal: only the $k=0$ term survives, so $c_0$ is the DC coefficient. Then look at a single cosine harmonic at the fundamental frequency; the same projection rule isolates that harmonic before any mixed signal adds extra bookkeeping.
You can read each coefficient as $c_k=|c_k|e^{j\angle c_k}$. The magnitude tells you how strong the harmonic is, and the angle tells you its phase shift.

sections.section_title: Evaluating One Complex Coefficient Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=4\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/3)$, compute $c_1$ from $c_1=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t}\,dt$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a single shifted cosine at the fundamental frequency, so the coefficient integral should isolate the matching $k=1$ harmonic. Rewrite the cosine in complex-exponential form first, then multiply by the matching exponential $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$.

After multiplication by $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, the $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ term becomes constant, while the other term becomes a $-2\omega_0$ exponential that averages to zero over one period. That is the orthogonality step that leaves only the matching harmonic behind.
So the integral isolates the $k=1$ harmonic and returns $c_1=2e^{-j\pi/3}$. That coefficient is the complex weight of the fundamental cosine term: its magnitude is $2$, and its angle is $-\pi/3$.

sections.section_title: Simplifying a Coefficient into Rectangular Form

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from $c_1=2e^{-j\pi/3}$, simplify the coefficient into rectangular form.

explanation_blocks.text: The only new wrinkle is the representation change. Use Euler's formula to rewrite the coefficient as a real part plus an imaginary part, then keep the magnitude $2$ outside the trigonometric terms.
Now substitute $\cos(-\pi/3)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin(-\pi/3)=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. That turns the exponential coefficient into a rectangular expression with the same harmonic weight.
So the coefficient in rectangular form is $c_1=1-j\sqrt{3}$. It is the same $k=1$ harmonic weight as before, just written as $a+jb$ instead of exponential form.

sections.section_title: Converting a Complex Coefficient to Magnitude and Phase

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_1=1-j\sqrt{3}$, convert it to magnitude and phase.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the rectangular coefficient $c_1=1-j\sqrt{3}$. The task is to read off its magnitude and its angle, because that polar pair is the amplitude-and-phase weight of the $k=1$ harmonic.
The real part is positive and the imaginary part is negative, so $c_1$ lies in quadrant IV. That means the phase is negative, with reference angle $\pi/3$ from the right triangle.
So the same harmonic weight is now written as magnitude $2$ with phase $-\pi/3$. This is the form used when you want to see how strongly the harmonic appears and what phase shift it carries.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Positive and Negative Harmonic Weights

example_content.example_prompt: For a real periodic signal with $c_2=1-j$ and $c_{-2}=1+j$, interpret what the positive and negative harmonic weights mean in the reconstruction.

explanation_blocks.text: Because the signal is real, the coefficients at $+2$ and $-2$ must be conjugates. The cue is the pair, and the rule is that one real harmonic stores its amplitude-and-phase weight across both signs.
Use that pair inside the synthesis sum. The two complex exponentials combine into one real oscillation, so they are not two separate harmonics.

So the positive-index coefficient carries the amplitude-phase information: magnitude $\sqrt{2}$ and phase $-\pi/4$. The negative-index coefficient is the conjugate partner that makes the reconstruction real, and together they represent one $k=2$ harmonic with amplitude $2\sqrt{2}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert computed complex Fourier series coefficients into a magnitude spectrum by calculating |c_k| at DC and each positive and negative harmonic and interpreting the stem plot as the periodic signal's harmonic strength distribution.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Magnitude Spectrum

image_slots.image_description: A centered stem plot of the magnitude spectrum with nonnegative stems at k=0, k=±1, and k=±2, a horizontal harmonic-index axis, and visible stem heights showing that the plot records |c_k| rather than phase or signed coefficient values.

blocks.text: The quantity to recognize here is the magnitude spectrum. It takes the complex Fourier coefficients $c_k$ from the previous step and replaces each one with its magnitude, so the spectrum height at harmonic index $k$ is always nonnegative.

Read the centered stem at $k=0$ as the DC magnitude $M_0 = |c_0|$. Read each stem at $k=\pm 1$, $\pm 2$, and so on as the magnitude of that positive or negative harmonic, so the plot records harmonic strength at each index.

This plot keeps strength and discards phase: two coefficients with different signs or angles can land at the same height if their absolute values match. That is the only idea needed here, and it is the basis for reading harmonic strength in the sections that follow.

sections.section_title: Computing Magnitudes of Complex Fourier Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_1=3-4j$ and $c_{-1}=3+4j$, compute $|c_1|$ and $|c_{-1}|$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a conjugate pair of complex Fourier coefficients. When you see $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$, the move is to convert each one into a magnitude using $|c_k|$ because the stem heights in a magnitude spectrum are nonnegative.

The result is the pair $(5, 5)$. Both harmonic stems have the same height, so this step shows how a conjugate pair can produce equal magnitude-spectrum values even though the complex coefficients differ in sign.

sections.section_title: Including the DC Coefficient in a Magnitude Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_0=6$, $c_1=2-2j$, and $c_{-1}=2+2j$, include the DC coefficient when listing the magnitude spectrum values.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the spectrum includes a zero-frequency term as well as a conjugate harmonic pair. Use the same magnitude rule for every index: the DC stem is $|c_0|$, and the harmonic stems are $|c_1|$ and $|c_{-1}|$.

In index order, the magnitude-spectrum values are $6$, $2\sqrt{2}$, and $2\sqrt{2}$. The DC term is included by the same absolute-value rule as the other coefficients; it is simply the $k=0$ stem height in the same nonnegative spectrum.

sections.section_title: Plotting Positive and Negative Harmonic Magnitudes

image_slots.image_description: A centered magnitude-spectrum stem plot with nonnegative stems at k=0, k=±1, and k=±2. Use stem heights 6 at k=0, 2\sqrt{2} at k=\pm1, and 1 at k=\pm2. Show a horizontal harmonic-index axis, a visible origin at the center, and mirrored positive and negative harmonic stems that all stay above or on the axis.

example_content.example_prompt: Given $|c_0|=6$, $|c_{\pm1}|=2\sqrt{2}$, and $|c_{\pm2}|=1$, draw the centered magnitude-spectrum stem plot.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the magnitudes are already known, so the job is to place them on a centered spectrum axis. Use the same magnitude rule as before, and put one nonnegative stem at each harmonic index.

Place the stem at $k=0$ with height $6$, the stems at $k=\pm1$ with height $2\sqrt{2}$, and the stems at $k=\pm2$ with height $1$. The finished plot is centered, symmetric across matching harmonic indices, and every stem stays nonnegative.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Harmonic Strengths from a Magnitude Spectrum

image_slots.image_description: A centered magnitude-spectrum stem plot with one dominant DC stem at $k=0$, equal smaller stems at $k=\pm1$, and zero-magnitude stems at $k=\pm2$. Keep the plot uncluttered, label the horizontal axis with harmonic index $k$, and make the vertical magnitude differences easy to compare so the learner can identify the strongest and absent harmonics at a glance.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a magnitude spectrum with stems $|c_0|=5$, $|c_{\pm1}|=2$, and $|c_{\pm2}|=0$, interpret which harmonic is strongest and which harmonic is absent.

explanation_blocks.text: Read the stems as a strength comparison, not as signed values. The tallest stem marks the dominant harmonic component, and any zero-height stem marks an absent harmonic.
Here, the DC component is strongest because $|c_0|=5$ is the tallest stem. The $\pm1$ harmonic pair is present but weaker, and the $\pm2$ harmonic pair is absent because its stems have height $0$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute and interpret the phase spectrum by extracting the argument of each nonzero complex Fourier series coefficient and aligning those phases with the corresponding positive and negative harmonics of a periodic continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Phase Spectrum

blocks.text: If the magnitude spectrum tells you how large each harmonic coefficient is, the phase spectrum tells you its angle. It extends the magnitude spectrum by recording one phase value at each harmonic index $k$.
For every nonzero coefficient, read the phase as $\phi_k = \arg(C_k)$ and keep that value attached to the same harmonic index $k$. That phase is part of the spectrum, not a separate object.
In the base case, if $C_1 = 3e^{-j\pi/4}$, then the phase-spectrum entry at harmonic $k=1$ is $\phi_1 = -\pi/4$. The coefficient still belongs to harmonic 1; only the angle is what you record.
For real-valued signals, positive and negative harmonics come in conjugate pairs, so their phases are opposite. Zero coefficients have no phase entry, so they are left out of the phase spectrum.

sections.section_title: Extracting Phase from a Nonzero Complex Coefficient

example_content.example_prompt: Given $C_2 = -1 - \sqrt{3}j$, compute the phase at harmonic $k=2$ and rewrite the coefficient in phase-angle form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a single complex coefficient written in rectangular form: $C_2 = -1 - \sqrt{3}j$. The rule from the tutorial is to read phase as $\phi_k = \arg(C_k)$, so the first job is to place the point on the complex plane and identify its quadrant.
Because both parts are negative, $C_2$ lies in quadrant III. The reference angle is $\pi/3$, so the principal argument is $\phi_2 = -2\pi/3$.
That phase is the phase-spectrum entry at harmonic $k=2$. To confirm it, rewrite the coefficient in phase-angle form using the same magnitude and angle.
So the final reading is: harmonic $k=2$ has phase $-2\pi/3$, and the coefficient is $2e^{-j2\pi/3}$. The phase stays attached to the harmonic index; the magnitude only sets the coefficient's size.

sections.section_title: Assigning Phases to Positive and Negative Harmonics

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a full coefficient table. Read each nonzero coefficient and attach its phase to the same harmonic index $k$. Here the DC term is $C_0 = 2$, so it contributes the phase entry $\phi_0 = 0$.
For the first harmonic pair, $C_1 = 3e^{j\pi/4}$ and $C_{-1} = 3e^{-j\pi/4}$ give opposite phases at $k=1$ and $k=-1$. That means $\phi_1 = \pi/4$ and $\phi_{-1} = -\pi/4$.
For the third harmonic pair, $C_3 = 4e^{-j\pi/2}$ and $C_{-3} = 4e^{j\pi/2}$ give $\phi_3 = -\pi/2$ and $\phi_{-3} = \pi/2$. The harmonic index stays attached to each phase entry.

The zero coefficients at $k=\pm2$ do not add phase entries, so the phase spectrum is organized by the nonzero indices only. Across $k=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$, the phase assignment is the one above, with no phase shown at $k=\pm2$.

sections.section_title: Leaving Zero Coefficients Out of the Phase Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Given $C_0 = 1$, $C_1 = 0$, $C_{-1} = 0$, $C_2 = 2e^{j\pi/5}$, and $C_{-2} = 2e^{-j\pi/5}$, state which harmonics appear in the phase spectrum and which harmonics are omitted.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the zero entries at $k=1$ and $k=-1$. A zero Fourier coefficient has no argument, so it does not get a phase label. Keep the phase spectrum sparse: include only harmonics with nonzero coefficients.
So the phase spectrum contains only $k=0,2,-2$. The harmonics $k=1$ and $k=-1$ are omitted entirely, not shown with placeholder phases, and the remaining nonzero pair still has opposite phases.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Phase Spectrum from Fourier Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Given $C_0 = -3$, $C_1 = 2e^{-j\pi/6}$, $C_{-1} = 2e^{j\pi/6}$, $C_2 = 0$, $C_{-2} = 0$, $C_3 = 5e^{j\pi/2}$, and $C_{-3} = 5e^{-j\pi/2}$, compute the phase spectrum and interpret the resulting harmonic phases.

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the coefficient table and extract phase only from the nonzero entries. The negative DC term $C_0 = -3$ has phase $\pi$, the pair at $k=\pm 1$ has phases $\mp\pi/6$, and the pair at $k=\pm 3$ has phases $\pm\pi/2$. The zeros at $k=\pm 2$ do not produce phase entries.

So the phase spectrum is sparse: it keeps $k=0, \pm 1, \pm 3$ and leaves out $k=\pm 2$ entirely. The interpretation is direct: every nonzero harmonic carries a phase shift, the conjugate pair has opposite signs, and zero coefficients disappear from the phase spectrum instead of being given a placeholder value.
